Right: the returned tree of bags, each bag a shaded box holding one triangle: {A,B,E}, {B,C,E}, and {C,D,E}, joined in a chain; neighboring bags share two nodes, and every cycle edge lies inside a bag. The largest bag has 3 nodes, so the card gives the width 3 − 1 = 2." width="100%"} A tree decomposition arranges the nodes into overlapping groups called *bags*, connected as a tree, so that every edge lies inside some bag and the bags containing any given node form a connected piece of the tree. Its *width* is the size of the largest bag minus one, and the treewidth of the graph is the smallest width possible: trees have treewidth 1, cycles 2, and a complete graph on $n$ nodes $n - 1$. Many NP-hard problems (coloring, independent sets, probabilistic inference in graphical models) become fast on graphs of small treewidth when solved bag by bag along the decomposition. Computing the exact treewidth is NP-hard, so this method uses a greedy elimination heuristic, as NetworkX does, and the width it reports is an upper bound: - `"min_fill_in"` (default): eliminate the node whose neighbors need the fewest extra edges to become a clique. Usually tighter. - `"min_degree"`: eliminate a node of smallest degree. Faster. Edge direction, self-loops and parallel edges are ignored. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [heuristic]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [["min_fill_in"]{.st}]{.doc-parameter-default} : `"min_fill_in"` (default) or `"min_degree"`. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [tuple[int, Graph]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The width, and the decomposition as a new undirected tree whose nodes are the bags. Each bag is labeled with its members, such as `"{A,B,C}"`, and stores their node IDs in the node attribute `"bag"`. An empty graph has width `-1` and a single empty bag. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `heuristic=` is unknown. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Elimination repeatedly picks a node by the heuristic, joins its remaining neighbors into a clique (the "fill-in" edges), records the node with its neighbors, and removes it; elimination stops once the remaining nodes form a clique, which becomes the first bag. Undoing the eliminations in reverse, each node and its recorded neighbors form a new bag, attached to an existing bag that contains those neighbors. Min-degree uses a heap, while min-fill-in recomputes fill-in counts for every node at each step, so it is slower, roughly $O(V^2 \Delta^2)$ for maximum degree $\Delta$. Ties are broken by node ID; the widths match NetworkX's. ## Examples {.doc-examples} A cycle has treewidth 2. Its decomposition is a chain of bags of three nodes: ::: {#71c84983 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec ring = ec.Graph().add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E"]) ring.add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "D"), ("D", "E"), ("E", "A")]) width, tree = ring.tree_decomposition() width, [tree.get_label_from_id(n) for n in sorted(tree.get_node_ids(limit=None))] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (2, ['{C,D,E}', '{B,C,E}', '{A,B,E}']) ``` ::: ::: Every edge of the original graph sits inside some bag, and the bags form a tree: ::: {#34fb52b6 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} tree.is_tree(), tree.count_nodes() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (True, 3) ``` ::: ::: A tree has width 1, since each bag only needs a node and its parent: ::: {#e9f1c0d4 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} star = ec.Graph().add_star_graph(5) star.tree_decomposition(heuristic="min_degree")[0] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` 1 ``` ::: :::
